title: Speedy's showgirl career, Ain't Misbehavin' on her piano and Pittsburgh
summary: She was a straight lady at the Apollo, knew Lena Horne and Fats Waller, and had a Chicken Shack in Pittsburgh.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Didn't you tell me that Speedy had been an actress at one point?
Yes. Well, like a straight lady. Okay, let me back up awhile. Like on stage, when they used to have comedians, and it was always a pretty straight lady.
Because she was -- she was photogenic
and everything, because they used to run her picture in the Daily News, the New York Daily News, every day, you know, for advertisement. She -- I still have those pictures.

Well, it was the club, really, mainly. Maybe Connie's Inn or the Cotton Club or something like that, you know. And they would pick out the one that had the best shot, you know, picture, that is. But she would play the straight lady onstage, like at the Apollo, uptown, and the Alhambra, in those days, you know. And the old timers like Pigmeat, Pigmeat Markham, Dusty Fletcher. Gee whiz, I can't think of the rest of them. Maybe she did some work with (inaudible), too. But she knew Bert Williams. She never worked with him but she knew him. And gee -- oh, incidentally, 'Ain't Misbehavin'', was written on her piano. Fats Waller was on his way downtown Broadway, to get an advance from the publisher, so he and Andy Razaf and Harry Brooks, who was the third writer, they stopped off at Speedy's apartment, and Fats had his White Horse scotch, and they did, 'Ain't Misbehavin'' right on her piano. She didn't know it until Andy Razaf told me, before he died. Yeah, she didn't know what they were doing, because it hadn't grown into the hit it was, you know? But just while you're writing it, you know. And yeah, Fats used to -- and all those guys, she knew all those people. I remember the first time she asked me, she said, 'Do you want to meet --,' she knew I was an Ellington fan. She said, 'Do you want to meet

Duke?" And I said, "No, I'll meet him on my own terms, because she was going to invite him to dinner, because she knew him. Oh, she knew him that well, you know. And then when she moved to Pittsburgh, she had married the editor of the Pittsburgh Courier at that time, and she lived on the same -- oh, in the same apartment building with Lena, you know, the upstairs and downstairs. She used to nurse Lena's son, young Teddy that died, you know? And they knew -- they used to dance together. They knew each other very well. But she just couldn't take it. She couldn't take Pittsburgh and she went on back to New York. She was just a showgirl at heart. She was a swinger. She loved New York, that's all. Which I can understand, because I loved New York.
When was that? What year was she in Pittsburgh?
Oh, let's see. Maybe in the late '30s, or 40-ish, somewhere around there.
Uh-huh, '45, a year before Eubie Blake, because we were like -- I don't know whether I was the best man or what. But he and Marion got married the year after Speedy and I did, you know?
Didn't Speedy also have a restaurant or something in Pittsburgh?
Yes, she did. The Chicken Shack. She -- that's when she could really fry -- oh, boy, she could really

fry some chicken. And I think that's one of the reasons I -- kind of stayed there. I didn't mean to make a big thing out of it, but I just couldn't get away, you know? And we turned out to be very good friends, you know?
